ABSTRACT
Advances in 3D-printing technology have enabled the fabrication of periodic microstructures that exhibit characteristic mechan-
ical performances. In response, multiscale topology optimization, which finds the optimal design of microstructure for the
macrostructure geometry and performance requirements, has become a hot topic in the field of structural optimization. While
the basic optimization framework based on the homogenization theory spanning macro and microscales is available, it is com-
putationally expensive and not easily applicable in practical scenarios such as high-resolution design for precision modeling and
reliable design considering non-linearities. To address this issue, we focus on a homogenization analysis using a fast Fourier trans-
form as an alternative approach to conventional finite element analysis and develop an optimization method with fast computing
speed and low memory requirements. In this paper, we define a simple stiffness maximization problem with linear elastic materials
and conduct two and three-dimensional optimization analyses to evaluate the validity and performance of the proposed method.
We discuss the advantages of computational cost, the influence of the filtering process, and the appropriate setting of material
contrast.

Introduction
Topology optimization [1, 2] is a numerical design method for
finding optimal structures that maximize or control certain per-
formance, and the developments of additive manufacturing tech-
nology have made it feasible and practical [3]. In recent years,
topology optimization has been applied to designing periodic
microstructures (lattice structures) and studied intensively [4] to
acquire further mechanical performance that cannot be achieved
with uniform solids.
The optimal design of microstructures originated from the
inverse homogenization approach, which obtains microstruc-
tures with prescribed homogenized properties proposed by

Rodrigues et al. [11] proposed a hierarchical approach to
obtain an optimal microstructure in each finite element of the
macrostructure, which was later extended to a three-dimensional
design by Coelho et al. [12]. However, this approach lacks con-
nectivity and manufacturability due to the existence of many dif-
ferent microstructures. Liu et al. [13] defined an optimization
problem where the macrostructure consists of a single, uniform
microstructure and optimized topologies at both scales using an
interpolation scheme called the PAMP method, a variant of the
SIMP method [14] for the macroscale. As an application of this
scheme, they also demonstrated maximization of the fundamen-
tal frequency at the macroscale [15]. Yan et al. [16] adopted
the bi-directional evolutionary structural optimization (BESO)
method [17], an alternative approach with discrete design vari-
ables, for concurrent multiscale optimization. Xia and Breitkopf
[18] introduced an optimization scheme for designing both scales
simultaneously using nested FEM (FE2 method [19]) based on a
non-linear multiscale analysis framework; Nakshatrala et al. [20]
also performed concurrent multiscale optimization for structures
composed of hyperelastic materials in a similar way.
To achieve the above-mentioned multiscale topology optimiza-
tion, it is necessary to simultaneously find a solution that sat-
isfies equilibrium at both scales based on homogenization the-
ory. However, since the number of stress evaluation points in the
macrostructure requires microstructure analyses, the computa-
tional effort of micro-macro coupled analysis is enormous. To
remedy this problem, Terada et al. [21] proposed a method called
micro and macro decoupling multiscale analysis, which analyzes
the micro and macro boundary value problems separately by
identifying the material parameters in a predefined macroscale
constitutive law through a procedure named numerical material
test. Kato et al. [22] applied the decoupling multiscale analysis to
topology optimization and proposed a simple and efficient imple-
mentation with an explicit sensitivity analysis scheme. They later
applied this scheme to the design of composite microstructures
with hyperelastic materials [23] by identifying macroscale con-
stitutive law using the differential evolution scheme [24].
However, even with efficient decoupling schemes, it is still chal-
lenging to utilize multiscale topology optimization for practical
structural design due to computational cost (compute time and
memory requirements). For example, analyses with non-linear
materials are demanded for designs that faithfully consider the
behavior of actual materials, but it requests a huge amount of
compute time to perform iterative non-linear analyses. In the
paper introduced above, Kato et al. [23] presented numerical
examples using a mesh of minimal resolution (103 = 1000 ele-
ments) for concurrent multiscale optimization with hyperelas-
tic materials due to computing time constraints. In addition,
structural analyses with sufficiently fine meshes for modeling
accuracy are necessary to fabricate optimized structures with a
3D-printer, but a significant increase in memory requirements
for increasing mesh resolution is inevitable as long as implicit
FEM is used. More specifically, a structural analysis with 1003 =
1, 000, 000 elements (8-node hexahedral elements) requires more
than 100 GB of memory; the available memory amount con-
strains the maximum mesh resolution of the microstructure. In
summary, computational cost is a bottleneck that prevents practi-
cal utilizations of multiscale topology optimization for structural
design.
As a side note, as the review article by Wu et al. [4] intro-
duces, there are various studies on acquiring optimized struc-
tures with less computational cost. One of the approaches is
to find an optimal arrangement of a set of microstructures
prepared in advance as functionally graded materials [25, 26].
Another approach is de-homogenization [27, 28], which maps
a predefined microstructure on an optimized macrostructure to
obtain a smooth, manufacturable structure. However, the pre-
pared microstructures are limited to simple geometries, such as
typical lattice structures, isotropic patterns maximizing bulk or
shear modulus, and truss structures with designated rank, result-
ing in relatively less design flexibility compared to the optimiza-
tion approaches that design microstructures based on multiscale
analysis, as introduced in the previous paragraphs.
To address the issue of computational cost in multiscale topol-
ogy optimization, we focus on homogenization analysis based on
fast Fourier transform (FFT), which originated from Moulinec
and Suquet [29, 30]. The FFT-based analysis was developed as an
efficient, alternative approach to previous FEM for solving peri-
odic composite microstructures with linear or non-linear materi-
als. In this method, mechanical fields such as strain and stress
are represented in the frequency domain (Fourier space), and
the equilibrium of the microstructure is solved iteratively by
alternating between the real and Fourier spaces. Mathematically,
this method reformulates the boundary value problem under
periodic boundary conditions into the Lippmann–Schwinger
equation, which is then solved using fixed-point iteration via FFT
to compute the unknown strain field at equilibrium. The simple
data structure with pixel or voxelwise discretization and itera-
tive algorithm without solving simultaneous equations make it
superior in terms of computational cost. Several research groups
[31–33] proposed similar improved algorithms in order to miti-
gate convergence deterioration in cases with high ratios between
maximum and minimum values of Young’s modulus called phase
contrast. In addition, various enhanced schemes were developed
such as algorithms applying the conjugate gradient method [34,
35] and fast gradient method [36]. Willot [37] introduced a mod-
ified Green operator, while Schneider et al. [38] and Leuschner
and Fritzen [39] included advanced discretization; they acquired
better local accuracy, removing Gibbs artifacts. For further details
on FFT-based analysis, refer to the comprehensive review paper
by Lucarini et al. [40]. Although these studies are aimed at accel-
erating standard structural analysis of microstructure, features
such as an analysis domain defined with a structured mesh and
an advantage in computational costs suggest compatibility with
multiscale topology optimization.
While most studies on topology optimization are based on
FEM, Chen et al. [41] utilized FFT-based analysis to design
microstructures focusing on its advantages. They adopted the
original algorithm by Moulinec and Suquet [29], the so-called
basic scheme, and presented optimization examples with around
one million voxels using the BESO method. However, this
study designed only microstructures without considering the
macroscale based on inverse homogenization; isotropic opti-
mized structures focusing on homogenized properties such as
bulk modulus and Poisson’s ratio are not optimal with respect
to a specific macrostructure. There was no validation based on
comparisons with the conventional FEM approach or detailed
discussions in terms of computational cost.

With these circumstances, in this study, we develop an efficient
multiscale topology optimization by applying FFT-based analy-
sis. To be specific, based on the framework of multiscale topology
optimization proposed by Kato et al. [22], we aim to accelerate the
optimization process by replacing analysis for the microstructure
with the algorithm introduced by Eyre and Milton [31]. We define
an optimization problem of a microstructure to maximize the lin-
ear stiffness of a macrostructure, one of the most basic design
problems, and conduct two and three-dimensional optimization
analyses for comparison of the proposed FFT-based and conven-
tional FEM-based approaches. First, we validate that the FFT
approach can reliably yield optimized structures same as the FEM
approach, by using a density filter. Then, we investigate the com-
putational cost and demonstrate quantitatively that the proposed
approach is superior, especially for three-dimensional designs
with high-resolution meshes. In addition, we discuss appropri-
ate choices for the contrast between two materials in the design
of porous microstructures consisting of void and solid material.
The remaining parts of this paper are as follows: Section 2
first explains an outline of decoupling multiscale analysis, and
Section 3 then describes algorithms of FFT-based analyses. An
interpolation scheme for materials and a stiffness maximization
problem are defined in Section 4. Section 5 presents numerical
examples to evaluate the validity and performance of the pro-
posed FFT-based optimization. Finally, a conclusion is summa-
rized in Section 6.

Decoupling Multiscale Analysis
The analysis used in this study is based on a decoupling
multiscale analysis method that solves the macro and micro
boundary value problems separately. This method considers
a homogeneous body equivalent to an inhomogeneous peri-

macrostructure has its material properties. While the decoupling
scheme is particularly effective for analysis with non-linear mate-
rials [23, 42], in the case of linear elasticity, the homogeneous
body can be represented using homogenized elasticity, result-
ing in no significant difference from the classical homogeniza-
tion approach. Nevertheless, it offers the advantage of simpler
sensitivity analysis derivation and implementation in topology
optimization. Figure 1 is a schematic image and illustrates the

Conclusion
This study developed a multiscale topology optimization apply-
ing FFT-based analysis to reduce the computational costs
of conventional approaches. Optimization analyses for perfor-
mance comparison of the proposed FFT-based and conventional
FEM-based approaches revealed the following. A simple den-
sity filter helps the FFT approach eliminate locally complex
structures and consistently yield the same optimized structure
as the FEM approach. The FFT approach is superior to the
FEM approach in computing time and memory requirements,
especially for three-dimensional designs with high-resolution
meshes, which can acquire more smooth structures with bet-
ter objective functions than lower-resolution cases. Even in the
design of porous microstructures consisting of void and solid
material, where the convergence of FFT-based analysis deterio-
rates, the proposed approach is still available by determining the
contrast between the two materials appropriately.

Abstract: Advances in 3D-printing technology have enabled the fabrication of periodic microstructures that exhibit characteristic mechan- ical performances. In response, multiscale topology optimization, which finds the optimal design of microstructure for the macrostructure geometry and performance requirements, has become a hot topic in the field of structural optimization. While the basic optimization framework based on the homogenization theory spanning macro and microscales is available, it is com- putationally expensive and not easily applicable in practical scenarios such as high-resolution design for precision modeling and reliable design considering non-linearities. To address this issue, we focus on a homogenization analysis using a fast Fourier trans- form as an alternative approach to conventional finite element analysis and develop an optimization method with fast computing speed and low memory requirements. In this paper, we define a simple stiffness maximization problem with linear elastic materials and conduct two and three-dimensional optimization analyses to evaluate the validity and performance of the proposed method. We discuss the advantages of computational cost, the influence of the filtering process, and the appropriate setting of material contrast.
